author: Alex Berger
title: Troy City Council passes Flock regulation, mayor plans to veto - NewsBreak
text:
By Alex Berger ,
56 minutes ago
TROY, N.Y. ( NEWS10 ) -- Troy City Council has passed Local Law 3, proposed by fourth district City Councilwoman Noreen McKee. This law regulates data from the city's Flock Safety automated license plate readers (ALPRs).
Download our WTEN+ streaming app on Roku, Fire TV and Apple TV! "We did a lot of research and I feel good about it," said McKee. "I think it's a good, good bill. And like I said, we can amend it. It's the beginning. It's not perfect. We're going to monitor it."
Local Law 3 limits the data storage window to 72 hours. That window was originally 30 days. It'll also restrict how the data from the cameras is shared, and only allows for searches regarding felony investigations.
The council worked with the police department to monitor crimes within a 60-day window that incorporate the use of Flock technology. Within those 60 days, 30 crimes were reported, 29 of them within 48-hours. One crime was reported within a 72-hour window, thus the storage window was proposed as 72 hours.
"We discovered that there's a fine line between a serious misdemeanor and a felony," said McKee. "So we decided to change the language, loosen it up a bit, and we said related to or involved in a felony."
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox! All six speakers who took to the podium for public comment were not satisfied.
"This is not the end of the movement to stop Flock in Troy," said Bryan Paz-Hernandez, a Troy resident. "We want the Flock cameras taken down."
Roughly an hour from Troy, Dutchess County canceled their contract with Flock; a move many Troy residents want to see in their city.
"In Dutchess County, the D.A. and the sheriff listened to their constituents," said Frances Sweet, a Troy resident. "The people said they didn't want the cameras and those officials withdrew their support for them."
Residents are also concerned that information from the cameras could be shared with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). On their website , Flock says they don't work with ICE. The information posted on the website states that sharing with federal agencies is disabled by default, but communities can allow federal data access.
"Decisions about whether, when, and how data is shared are made by the customer that owns the data, not by Flock," the website reads. "There is no hidden back-door access in Flock technology."
East Greenbush speakers have difference of opinions on Flock cameras Mayor Carmella Mantello said they do not give their video to the federal government.
"The reason the prior administration procured Flock is because they do not share it with federal agencies, including ICE," she said. "To date, that continues."
The police department has to tell the council after 90 days how the law is working. But, Mantello said she plans to take the measures to veto Local Law 3.
